children: Ryanair Holdings expects a significantly higher fuel bill for its next fiscal year and is looking at potential cost cuts to soften the blow, warning that hiking prices and pulling routes won't be enough.

The conflict in the Middle East has pushed up fuel costs for airlines around the world, prompting carriers to raise fares and trim routes at a time when many customers are holding off on booking tickets until the last minute due to economic uncertainty.

"Unless there is a swift resolution of the Middle East conflict, we expect jet-fuel prices to remain elevated well into 2027," Ryanair Chief Executive Michael O'Leary said Monday. "As low-cost oil hedges roll off ahead of [the summer of 2027], all EU airlines face a significantly higher fuel bill next year."

European short-haul fares are expected to increase materially due to higher jet-fuel prices and capacity cuts at airlines, but this is still unlikely to fully counter an estimated increase of around 2 billion euros ($2.23 billion) in Ryanair's fuel bill for the year ending March 2028, based on current forward prices, the Dublin-based airline group said.
The company said it is looking at airport negotiations, maturing labor agreements, lower crewing ratios and the use of artificial intelligence to drive savings.

Ryanair recently cut its passenger-traffic forecast for its current fiscal year to reduce its exposure to unhedged fuel. It expects traffic for fiscal 2028 to rise 3% to 220 million passengers, as it anticipates that the European Union Aviation Safety Agency will certify Boeing's 737 MAX 10 in the coming weeks, paving the way for its first 16 deliveries in the spring.

The company said its earnings for the year ending in March are well insulated from current oil-price volatility due to current hedges. While 80% of Ryanair's jet-fuel needs for fiscal 2027 are hedged at $65 a barrel, its fiscal 2028 hedge cover stands at 25%, hedged at $95 a barrel, it added.

Last quarter, the cost of unhedged jet fuel doubled, contributing to a jump in operating expenses that ate into the group's profit. Still, the company said it plans a share buyback of 800 million euros starting in February, and declared an interim dividend of 27.3 European cents a share, up from 19.3 cents a year before.

Ryanair said it made a pretax profit of 1.83 billion euros for the quarter ended Sept. 30 compared with 1.96 billion euros in the same period last year. Quarterly net profit dropped 6% to 1.61 billion euros.
A 10% rise in operating expenses offset an increase in revenue to 5.7 billion euros from 5.48 billion euros. Analysts polled by Visible Alpha had forecast revenue at 5.72 billion euros.

The company said demand is strong for the December quarter, with prices trending modestly ahead of the same time last year, but that Christmas and school midterm bookings will determine where quarterly fares land.
With limited visibility into the fourth quarter of the current fiscal year, it is too early to provide meaningful profit guidance for fiscal 2027, Ryanair added.
